According to the U.S. census, Ojibwe people are one of the largest tribal populations among [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") peoples in the U.S. In Canada, they are the second-largest [First Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Nations_in_Canada "First Nations in Canada") population, surpassed only by the [Cree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cree "Cree"). They are one of the most numerous [Indigenous peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") north of the [Rio Grande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Grande "Rio Grande").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-3)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] The Ojibwe population is approximately 320,000, with 170,742 living in the U.S. as of 2010 and approximately 160,000 in Canada.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-capop2-1) In the U.S. there are 77,940 mainline Ojibwe, 76,760 Saulteaux, and 8,770 Mississauga, organized in 125 bands. In Canada they live from western [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec") to eastern [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia").
The Ojibwe language is [Anishinaabemowin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe_language "Ojibwe language"), a branch of the [Algonquian language family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algonquian_languages "Algonquian languages").

The Ojibwe are part of the [Council of Three Fires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Three_Fires "Council of Three Fires") (along with the [Odawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people "Odawa people") and [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi")) and of the larger Anishinaabeg, which includes [Algonquin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algonquin_people "Algonquin people"), [Nipissing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nipissing_First_Nation "Nipissing First Nation"), and Oji-Cree people. Historically, through the Saulteaux branch, they were part of the [Iron Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Confederacy "Iron Confederacy"), with the Cree, [Assiniboine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assiniboine "Assiniboine"), and [Metis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9tis "Métis").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-:0-4)

The [dreamcatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreamcatcher "Dreamcatcher") originated from the Ojibwe and became a popular commercial item in the late 20th century and became a symbol for the [Pan-Indian movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-Indianism "Pan-Indianism").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-5) The Ojibwe are known for their [birchbark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birchbark "Birchbark")[canoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canoe "Canoe"), [birchbark scrolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birchbark_scrolls "Birchbark scrolls"), mining and trade in [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper"), and their harvesting of [wild rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_rice "Wild rice") and [maple syrup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maple_syrup "Maple syrup").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-6) Their [Midewiwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midewiwin "Midewiwin") Society is well respected as the keeper of detailed and complex scrolls of events, oral history, songs, maps, memories, stories, geometry, and mathematics.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-7)[_[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]
European powers, Canada, and the U.S. have colonized Ojibwe lands. The Ojibwe signed treaties with settler leaders to share land for the survival of settlers in exchange for compensation, according to Midewiwin laws pre-dating European contact, with an expectation of mutual non-interference. Many European settlers moved into the Ojibwe ancestral lands.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-capop2-1)

Ojibwa women in a canoe at [Leech Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leech_Lake "Leech Lake"), [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota"), in 1909
The [exonym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exonym_and_endonym "Exonym and endonym") for this Anishinaabe group is _Ojibwe_ (plural: _Ojibweg_). This word has two variations, one French (Ojibwa) and the other English (Chippewa).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-8) Although [many variations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwa_ethnonyms "Ojibwa ethnonyms") exist in the literature, _Chippewa_ is more common in the United States, and _Ojibway_ predominates in Canada,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-9) but both terms are used in each country. In many Ojibwe communities throughout Canada and the U.S. since the late 20th century, more members have been using the generalized name _Anishinaabe(-g)_.
The meaning of the name _Ojibwe_ is not known; the most common explanations for the name's origin are:

*   _ojiibwabwe_ (/o/ + /jiibw/ + /abwe/), meaning "those who cook/roast until it puckers", referring to their fire-curing of [moccasin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moccasin_(footwear) "Moccasin (footwear)") seams to make them waterproof.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-10) Some 19th century sources say this name described a method of ritual torture that the Ojibwe applied to enemies.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-11)  
*   _ozhibii'iwe_ (/o/ + /zhibii'/ + /iwe/), meaning "those who keep records [of a Vision]", referring to their form of [pictorial writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe_writing_systems "Ojibwe writing systems"), and [pictographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pictograph "Pictograph") used in Midewiwin sacred rites;[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-12) or  
*   _ojiibwe_ (/o/ + /jiib/ + /we/), meaning "those who speak stiffly" or "those who stammer", an exonym or name given to them by the [Cree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cree "Cree"), who described the Ojibwe language for its differences from their own.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-13)

**William Rufus DeVane King** (April 7, 1786 – April 18, 1853) was an American politician and diplomat who served as the 13th [vice president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_president_of_the_United_States "Vice president of the United States") from March 4, 1853, until his death. He previously served as a [U.S. representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") from [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), a [U.S. senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._senator "U.S. senator") from [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"), and [minister to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Ambassador_to_France "United States Ambassador to France").

A [Democratic-Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic-Republican_Party "Democratic-Republican Party") and later a [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), King was a leading political figure in early Alabama and was elected as one of the state's first U.S. senators after its admission to the Union in 1819. He aligned politically with [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson") and served multiple terms in the Senate, including as [president pro tempore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_pro_tempore_of_the_United_States_Senate "President pro tempore of the United States Senate"). During the sectional disputes preceding the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), he supported [slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery "Slavery") and opposed [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionist "Abolitionist") efforts in the territories, while also opposing [secession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession "Secession").
King was elected vice president in 1852 on the ticket headed by [Franklin Pierce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Pierce "Franklin Pierce"). Because he was ill with [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis"), Congress permitted him to take the oath of office in [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captaincy_General_of_Cuba "Captaincy General of Cuba"), making him the only U.S. vice president to be sworn in on foreign soil. He died 45 days later, without carrying out any duties of the office. Historians have also written about his close relationship with [James Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Buchanan "James Buchanan").

King was born on April 7, 1786, in [Sampson County, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampson_County,_North_Carolina "Sampson County, North Carolina"), the son of William King and Margaret DeVane. He graduated from the [University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Carolina_at_Chapel_Hill "University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill") in 1803, where he was a member of the [Philanthropic Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialectic_and_Philanthropic_Societies "Dialectic and Philanthropic Societies"). After [reading law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading_law "Reading law") with Judge William Duffy of [Fayetteville, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fayetteville,_North_Carolina "Fayetteville, North Carolina"), he was admitted to the bar in 1805 or 1806 and began practicing law in [Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton,_North_Carolina "Clinton, North Carolina").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-:0-2) King was also a [Freemason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freemasonry "Freemasonry").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-3)

[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/William_R._King%2C_Senator_from_Alabama_LCCN2003656251_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-William_R._King%2C_Senator_from_Alabama_LCCN2003656251_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:William_R._King,_Senator_from_Alabama_LCCN2003656251_(cropped).jpg)
Lithograph of King, c.1840
King was appointed [Minister to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Ambassador_to_France "United States Ambassador to France"), serving from 1844 to 1846. After his return, he resumed Senate service, first by appointment and then by election to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of [Arthur P. Bagby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_P._Bagby "Arthur P. Bagby"). He held his seat from July 1, 1848, until his resignation on December 20, 1852, due to ill health and his election as vice president of the United States.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-:1-8)

During the debates leading up to the [Compromise of 1850](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compromise_of_1850 "Compromise of 1850"), King supported the Senate [gag rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gag_rule "Gag rule") against debate on antislavery petitions and opposed proposals to abolish slavery in the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_of_Columbia "District of Columbia"), which Congress administered.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-alher-9) King supported slavery, arguing that the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States") protected the institution of slavery in both the Southern states and the [federal territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territories_of_the_United_States "Territories of the United States"). He opposed both [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionism_in_the_United_States "Abolitionism in the United States") efforts to abolish slavery in the territories and [Fire-Eater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire-Eaters "Fire-Eaters") calls for Southern [secession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession "Secession").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-senate.gov-10)

On July 11, 1850, two days after President [Zachary Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zachary_Taylor "Zachary Taylor") died, King was appointed Senate [President pro tempore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_pro_tempore_of_the_United_States_Senate "President pro tempore of the United States Senate"). When [Millard Fillmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millard_Fillmore "Millard Fillmore") became president, the vice presidency was vacant, making King first in the [line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession") under the law in effect. He also served as Chairman of the [Senate Committee on Foreign Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Foreign_Relations "United States Senate Committee on Foreign Relations").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-:0-2)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-:1-8)

## Relationship with James Buchanan
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_R._King&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Relationship with James Buchanan")]
[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/JamesBuchanan_crop.jpg/250px-JamesBuchanan_crop.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JamesBuchanan_crop.jpg)
[James Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Buchanan "James Buchanan"), 15th [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") (served 1857–1861). He shared a [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") boardinghouse with his friend and colleague, William R. King.

## Relationship with James Buchanan
However, historian Lewis Saum argued that customs and expressions in the mid-19th century differed from those of the present, and that "Miss Nancy" was "a fairly common designation for people who wore clean clothes and had good manners." He also noted that Brown was a political rival of King. Loewen described Buchanan and King as "Siamese twins".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-16)
Sol Barzman, a biographer of vice presidents, wrote that King's "fastidious habits and conspicuous intimacy with the bachelor Buchanan gave rise to some cruel jibes." Buchanan adopted King's mannerisms and romanticized southern culture. Both had strong political ambitions, and in 1844, they planned to run together for president and vice president.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-ReferenceB-13) They spent some time apart while King was on overseas missions in France, and their letters remain cryptic and do not reveal any personal feelings.
In May 1844, Buchanan wrote to Cornelia Roosevelt:
> I am now 'solitary and alone', having no companion in the house with me. I have gone a wooing to several gentlemen, but have not succeeded with any one of them. I feel that it is not good for man to be alone, and [I] should not be astonished to find myself married to some old maid who can nurse me when I am sick, provide good dinners for me when I am well, and not expect from me any very ardent or romantic affection.
After King died on April 18, 1853, at age 67, Buchanan described him as "among the best, the purest, and most consistent public men I have known".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-ReferenceB-13)
Baker concluded that, while some of their correspondence was destroyed by family members, the length and intimacy of the surviving letters illustrate "the affection of a special friendship" between King and Buchanan, with no way to determine whether it was a romantic relationship.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-17)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_R._King&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Vice presidency and death (1853)")]

Sharkey").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-senate.gov-10)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-harpers-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-aoc-vp-20) King was the first and, to date, only vice president or president of the United States to take the oath of office on foreign soil.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-21)

**William Rufus DeVane King** (April 7, 1786 – April 18, 1853) was an American politician and diplomat who served as the 13th [vice president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_president_of_the_United_States "Vice president of the United States") from March 4, 1853, until his death. He previously served as a [U.S. representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") from [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), a [U.S. senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._senator "U.S. senator") from [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"), and [minister to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Ambassador_to_France "United States Ambassador to France").
texts.4:
A [Democratic-Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic-Republican_Party "Democratic-Republican Party") and later a [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), King was a leading political figure in early Alabama and was elected as one of the state's first U.S. senators after its admission to the Union in 1819. He aligned politically with [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson") and served multiple terms in the Senate, including as [president pro tempore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_pro_tempore_of_the_United_States_Senate "President pro tempore of the United States Senate"). During the sectional disputes preceding the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), he supported [slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery "Slavery") and opposed [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionist "Abolitionist") efforts in the territories, while also opposing [secession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession "Secession").
King was elected vice president in 1852 on the ticket headed by [Franklin Pierce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Pierce "Franklin Pierce"). Because he was ill with [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis"), Congress permitted him to take the oath of office in [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captaincy_General_of_Cuba "Captaincy General of Cuba"), making him the only U.S. vice president to be sworn in on foreign soil. He died 45 days later, without carrying out any duties of the office. Historians have also written about his close relationship with [James Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Buchanan "James Buchanan").
texts.5: King was born on April 7, 1786, in [Sampson County, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampson_County,_North_Carolina "Sampson County, North Carolina"), the son of William King and Margaret DeVane. He graduated from the [University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Carolina_at_Chapel_Hill "University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill") in 1803, where he was a member of the [Philanthropic Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialectic_and_Philanthropic_Societies "Dialectic and Philanthropic Societies"). After [reading law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading_law "Reading law") with Judge William Duffy of [Fayetteville, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fayetteville,_North_Carolina "Fayetteville, North Carolina"), he was admitted to the bar in 1805 or 1806 and began practicing law in [Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton,_North_Carolina "Clinton, North Carolina").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-:0-2) King was also a [Freemason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freemasonry "Freemasonry").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-3)

[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/William_R._King%2C_Senator_from_Alabama_LCCN2003656251_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-William_R._King%2C_Senator_from_Alabama_LCCN2003656251_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:William_R._King,_Senator_from_Alabama_LCCN2003656251_(cropped).jpg)

King was appointed [Minister to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Ambassador_to_France "United States Ambassador to France"), serving from 1844 to 1846. After his return, he resumed Senate service, first by appointment and then by election to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of [Arthur P. Bagby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_P._Bagby "Arthur P. Bagby"). He held his seat from July 1, 1848, until his resignation on December 20, 1852, due to ill health and his election as vice president of the United States.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-:1-8)
texts.10: During the debates leading up to the [Compromise of 1850](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compromise_of_1850 "Compromise of 1850"), King supported the Senate [gag rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gag_rule "Gag rule") against debate on antislavery petitions and opposed proposals to abolish slavery in the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_of_Columbia "District of Columbia"), which Congress administered.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-alher-9) King supported slavery, arguing that the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States") protected the institution of slavery in both the Southern states and the [federal territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territories_of_the_United_States "Territories of the United States"). He opposed both [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionism_in_the_United_States "Abolitionism in the United States") efforts to abolish slavery in the territories and [Fire-Eater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire-Eaters "Fire-Eaters") calls for Southern [secession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession "Secession").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-senate.gov-10)
texts.11: On July 11, 1850, two days after President [Zachary Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zachary_Taylor "Zachary Taylor") died, King was appointed Senate [President pro tempore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_pro_tempore_of_the_United_States_Senate "President pro tempore of the United States Senate"). When [Millard Fillmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millard_Fillmore "Millard Fillmore") became president, the vice presidency was vacant, making King first in the [line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession") under the law in effect. He also served as Chairman of the [Senate Committee on Foreign Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Foreign_Relations "United States Senate Committee on Foreign Relations").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-:0-2)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-:1-8)

## Relationship with James Buchanan
However, historian Lewis Saum argued that customs and expressions in the mid-19th century differed from those of the present, and that "Miss Nancy" was "a fairly common designation for people who wore clean clothes and had good manners." He also noted that Brown was a political rival of King. Loewen described Buchanan and King as "Siamese twins".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-16)
Sol Barzman, a biographer of vice presidents, wrote that King's "fastidious habits and conspicuous intimacy with the bachelor Buchanan gave rise to some cruel jibes." Buchanan adopted King's mannerisms and romanticized southern culture. Both had strong political ambitions, and in 1844, they planned to run together for president and vice president.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-ReferenceB-13) They spent some time apart while King was on overseas missions in France, and their letters remain cryptic and do not reveal any personal feelings.
In May 1844, Buchanan wrote to Cornelia Roosevelt:
> I am now 'solitary and alone', having no companion in the house with me. I have gone a wooing to several gentlemen, but have not succeeded with any one of them. I feel that it is not good for man to be alone, and [I] should not be astonished to find myself married to some old maid who can nurse me when I am sick, provide good dinners for me when I am well, and not expect from me any very ardent or romantic affection.
After King died on April 18, 1853, at age 67, Buchanan described him as "among the best, the purest, and most consistent public men I have known".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-ReferenceB-13)
Baker concluded that, while some of their correspondence was destroyed by family members, the length and intimacy of the surviving letters illustrate "the affection of a special friendship" between King and Buchanan, with no way to determine whether it was a romantic relationship.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King#cite_note-17)

# U.S. Vice Presidents: Elbridge Gerry
## Biography
Elbridge Gerry, (born July 17, 1744,Marblehead,Massachusetts[U.S.]—died November 23, 1814, Washington,D.C., U.S.), signer of the American Declaration of Independence and fifth vice president of the United States(1813–14) in the second term of Pres.James Madison. From his name the term _gerrymander_ later was derived.
Born into a wealthy merchant family, Gerry vocally opposed British colonial policy in the 1760s and was active in the early stages of organizing the resistance in the American Revolutionary War. Elected to the Second Continental Congress, Gerry signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Articles of Confederation. He was one of three men who attended the Constitutional Convention in 1787 who refused to sign the United States Constitution because it did not then include a Bill of Rights. After its ratification he was elected to the inaugural United States Congress, where he was actively involved in drafting and passage of the Bill of Rights as an advocate of individual and state liberties.

### Involvement with the American Indian Movement
On [Thanksgiving Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thanksgiving_Day "Thanksgiving Day") 1970, Means and other AIM activists staged their first protest in Boston: they seized the _[Mayflower II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayflower\_II "Mayflower II")_, a replica ship of the [Mayflower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayflower "Mayflower"), to protest the Puritans' and United States' mistreatment of Native Americans.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Means#cite_note-pbs-8) In 1971 Means was one of the leaders of AIM's takeover of [Mount Rushmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rushmore "Mount Rushmore"), a federal monument. Rushmore is within the [Black Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills "Black Hills"), an area sacred to the Lakota tribe.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Means#cite_note-Means17-3)
In November 1972, he participated in AIM's occupation of the [Bureau of Indian Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_Indian_Affairs "Bureau of Indian Affairs") (BIA) headquarters in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), to protest abuses. Many records were taken or destroyed, and more than $2 million in damage was done to the building.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Means#cite_note-Means17-3)

### Involvement with the American Indian Movement
In 1973, [Dennis Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Banks "Dennis Banks") and Carter Camp led AIM's occupation of [Wounded Knee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wounded_Knee_incident "Wounded Knee incident"), which became the group's best-known action.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Means#cite_note-pbs-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Means#cite_note-9) Means appeared as a spokesman and prominent leader. The armed standoff of more than 300 Lakota and AIM activists with the [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") (FBI) and state law enforcement lasted for 71 days. Frank Clearwater, a visiting [Cherokee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee "Cherokee") activist from North Carolina, and Lawrence "Buddy" Lamont, an [Oglala Lakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oglala_Lakota "Oglala Lakota") activist from Pine Ridge Reservation, were killed in April. African-American activist [Ray Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Robinson_(activist) "Ray Robinson (activist)") disappeared and is assumed to be buried in the hills.

### Involvement with the American Indian Movement
#### Native American politics
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Means&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Native American politics")]
In 1974, Means resigned from AIM to run for the presidency of his native [Oglala Sioux Tribe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oglala_Sioux_Tribe "Oglala Sioux Tribe") (OST) against the incumbent [Richard Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Wilson_(tribal_chairman) "Dick Wilson (tribal chairman)"). The official vote count showed Wilson winning by more than 200 votes. Residents complained of intimidation by Wilson's private militia. The report of a government investigation confirmed problems in the election, but in a related court challenge to the results of the election, a federal court upheld the results.
In the late 1970s, Means turned to an international forum on issues of rights for [indigenous peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples "Indigenous peoples"). He worked with Jimmie Durham, who established the offices of the [International Indian Treaty Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Indian_Treaty_Council "International Indian Treaty Council") to work with the United Nations in 1977. At the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, he assisted in the organization of community institutions, such as the [KILI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KILI "KILI") radio station and the Porcupine Health Clinic in [Porcupine, South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porcupine,_South_Dakota "Porcupine, South Dakota").
Means also traveled to [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), traveled behind the [Iron Curtain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Curtain "Iron Curtain") to meet with [East German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Germany "East Germany") AIM supporters, and he traveled to Switzerland to take part in the Geneva human rights conference.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Means#cite_note-10)

### Involvement with the American Indian Movement
#### Native American politics
Means and Ojibwe [Dennis Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Banks "Dennis Banks") were by the mid-1970s the best known [Native Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") since [Lakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakota_people "Lakota people") war leaders [Sitting Bull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitting_Bull "Sitting Bull") and [Crazy Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_Horse "Crazy Horse"), who led the attack that defeated the forces of General [Custer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Armstrong_Custer "George Armstrong Custer") at [The Battle of Little Big Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Little_Bighorn "Battle of the Little Bighorn"), also known as [The Battle of the Greasy Grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Little_Bighorn "Battle of the Little Bighorn").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Means#cite_note-11)

### Involvement with the American Indian Movement
#### Native American politics
In the 1980s, AIM divided into several competing factions, in part over differences among members regarding support for the indigenous peoples in [Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua "Nicaragua"). Means supported the [Miskito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miskito_people "Miskito people") group MISURASATA (later known as [YATAMA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YATAMA "YATAMA")), which was allied with the [Contras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contras "Contras"). He traveled to Nicaragua in 1985 and 1986 on fact-finding tours. He came to believe that the Miskito as a people were being targeted for elimination.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Means#cite_note-McLellan-12) Some AIM members supported the [Sandinistas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandinista_National_Liberation_Front "Sandinista National Liberation Front") of the national government, although they had forced removal of thousands of Miskito from their traditional territory.
On January 8, 1988, Means held a press conference to announce his retirement from AIM, saying it had achieved its goals.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Means#cite_note-13) That January, the AIM Grand Governing Council, headed by the [Bellecourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clyde_Bellecourt "Clyde Bellecourt") brothers, released a press release noting this was the sixth resignation by Means since 1974, and asking the press to "never again report either that he is a founder of the American Indian Movement, or [that] he is a leader of the American Indian Movement". The AIM Grand Governing Council noted there were many open issues and legislation regarding Native Americans for which they were continuing to work.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Means#cite_note-14)

### Involvement with the American Indian Movement
#### Native American politics
In 1993, the organization divided officially into two main factions: AIM Grand Governing Council, based in Minnesota, which copyrighted the name American Indian Movement; and American Indian Movement Confederation of Autonomous Chapters, based in Colorado and allied with Means and [Ward Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ward_Churchill "Ward Churchill").
On November 3, 1999, Means and Robert Pictou-Branscombe, a maternal cousin of Aquash from Canada, held a press conference in Denver at the Federal Building to discuss the slow progress of the government's investigation into Aquash's murder. It had been under investigation both by the Denver police, as Aquash had been kidnapped from there, and by the [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI "FBI"), as she had been taken across state lines and killed on the Pine Ridge Reservation. Both Branscombe and Means accused [Vernon Bellecourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_Bellecourt "Vernon Bellecourt"), a high-ranking leader of AIM, of having ordered her execution. Means said that [Clyde Bellecourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clyde_Bellecourt "Clyde Bellecourt"), a founder of AIM, had ensured that it was carried out at the Pine Ridge Reservation. Means said that an AIM tribunal had banned the Bellecourt brothers but tried to keep the reason for the dissension internal to protect AIM.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Means#cite_note-press-15)

Vice President elected on 1860 Republican ticket but unexpectedly dropped on 1864 Union ticket in favor of Andrew Johnson, a Tennessee War Democrat. He had a cordial but not close relationship with the President. He exercised an important role in the selection of Lincoln’s first cabinet; he argued unsuccessfully against Seward’s inclusion in cabinet but was successful in naming Gideon Welles as New England’s cabinet representative. Hamlin played little role in President Lincoln’s first term, but did help win Mr. Lincoln’s agreement for the use of black soldiers. Hamlin was a strong supporter of Negro rights, before, during and after the Civil War. After the First Battle of Bull Run in July 1861, Hamlin became one of the first to pressure the President to pursue emancipation and recruitment of black soldiers as a strategy of war. He pushed for an immediate Proclamation of Emancipation in 1862.
White House etiquette did not even allow the Vice President regularly to attend cabinet meetings so unlike heads of departments, he seldom visited the White House—perhaps because he and Mary Todd Lincoln did not like each other. Aide William O. Stoddard noted: “It seems that a sort of etiquette has been established, in accordance with which it is not considered god taste for the second officer of the Republic to meddle much with public business, and which, at all events, keeps him away from the Executive Mansion.”1
Hamlin did not spend much more time in Washington during the war than necessary. He returned to Maine after his inauguration on March 4, 1861, proceeded to New York City after Fort Sumter fell, then returned to Maine, then back to New York and Washington. But he almost immediately returned to Maine, returning in time for the special session of Congress at the beginning of July. He later went to the White House. President Lincoln “was very busy, but treated me cordially and seemed pleased to see me. Hamlin and Senator James R. Doolittle had escorted Johnson to the Capitol. In the Senate chamber Hamlin gave a short, cogent speech before an unwell Johnson, fortified with whiskey, gave a long and incoherent one. Ironically, as vice president Hamlin had risked the fury of liquor-loving Senators by banning it from Senate chambers and thus had turned the Senate into a more decorous institution. Two of Hamlin’s children — Sarah and Charles — remained in Washington and were at Ford’s Theater on the night President Lincoln was assassinated five weeks later. Vice President-elect Hamlin and President-elect Lincoln Lincoln had first met in Chicago in late November 1860 when they discussed possible members of the Lincoln cabinet. Lincoln said to Hamlin of hearing him in 1848: “Your subject was not new, but the ideas were sound. You were talking about slavery, and I now take occasion to thank you for so well expressing what were my own sentiments at that time.” Hamlin recalled being told that Lincoln was “the best story teller in the House.”12

Hamlin’s sons Charles and Cyrus were both Union generals; Hamlin himself even served briefly as a private in the Army during the Civil War. Hamlin also served as Congressman (Democrat, 1853-47) Senator from Maine (Democrat, Republican, 1848-57, 57-61, 1869-81) and Governor (Republican, 1857). He was appointed Collector of the Port of Boston in 1865 but quit a year later in disagreement with President Johnson’s reconstruction policies. [![Image 1: Edward Duffield Neill](https://www.mrlincolnswhitehouse.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/pf096062_med.jpg)](https://www.mrlincolnswhitehouse.org/residents-visitors/employees-and-staff/employees-staff-edward-duffield-neill-1823-1893/edward-duffield-neill/index.html)
Assistant secretary to President Lincoln (1864-65), Edward Duffield Neill was an ordained Presbyterian minister and dedicated historian. At the beginning of the Civil War, Rev. Neill served as chaplain to a Minnesota regiment and later as an army hospital chaplain in Philadelphia.
Neill took on William Stoddard’s land patent duties after William Stoddard became ill in mid-1864. Lincoln biographer Carl Sandburg wrote: “Chaplain Neill came to Lincoln’s office with a Vermont colonel seeking a brigadier general’s commission Lincoln had signed. The President had not returned from lunch. Neill was looking among papers on the President’s desk. The President came in eating an apple. ‘I told him for what I was looking,’ wrote Neill of this, ‘and as I talked he placed his hand on the bell-pull, when I said, ‘For whom are you going to ring?’ Placing his hand upon my coat, he spoke but two words, – ‘Andrew Johnson.’ Then I said, ‘I will come in again.’ As I was leaving the room the Vice President had been ushered in, and the President advanced and took him by the hand.’”1 Secretaries John G. Nicolay and John Hayclearly trusted Neill, who was older than both of them. Leaving to meet with Horace Greeley in mid-July 1864, Hay wrote Edward Neill: “I am going to New York tonight on business. Will be gone only a very few days”
> I leave matters in your hands till my return. There will probably be little to do. Refer as little to the President as possible. Keep visitors out of the house when you can. Inhospitable, but prudent.  
>   
>  I have a few franked envelopes. Let matters of ordinary reference go without formality of signature. If you have any doubt about any matter, please reserve it till my return.2

On the day President Lincoln was assassinated — April 14, 1865 — Neill saw President about a commission for the Freedman’s Bureau. He wrote later that “The President’s capacity for work was wonderful. While other men were taking recreation through the sultry months of summer he remained in his office attending to the wants of the nation. He was never an idler or a lounger. Each hour he was busy.”3
“Every month my impression of the greatness of President Lincoln increased. He was above a life of mere routine. In his bearing there was nothing artificial or mechanical,” wrote Neill. “He was independent of all cliques. Willing to be convinced, with a wonderful patience he listened to the opinions and criticisms of others.”4 Neill was also a chronicler of the President’s human side, writing on May 31, 1864: “Yesterday four or five thousand Sunday School children, with banner and bands of music[,] marched by the President’s House, while he stood at the window and received their hearty cheers with smiles…”5
Neill was a decade older than the older presidential assistants and had considerable experience in church and education affairs – while the primary assistants had a background in writing, journalism and politics. But like his colleagues, Neill was protective of the President.

> One morning he told his doorkeeper that he should not be interrupted as he was much engaged. Senator Howard of Michigan, came and said he must see him. The doorkeeper could not disobey orders, and brought him to me. As soon as he sat down, he showed that he was in ill humor, and said: ‘If it were his own son he would not act so.’ Never having seen the Senator, and supposing him to be some agent to procure substitutes, I replied that if he continued to speak disrespectfully of the President, in his own house, I must request him to leave the room. He then said that he was Senator Howard, and that he had come to request suspension of sentence of a soldier who in a few hours was to be executed.  
>   
>  Entering the President’s room, I found him very busy in writing, and apologetically said: ‘Would not have interrupted you, but Senator Howard wants suspension of sentence, in a certain case.’ ‘Wants suspension! Well, that is a queer request.’ Afterward he told me to write a telegram, giving the soldier’s name, ordering suspension of sentence, sign his name, and send it through the War Department. I told him I would write the order, but preferred that he should sign it.6
Neill remained at the White House as an aide to President Andrew Johnson. Unlike Stoddard, whom he replaced, Neill was a moderate on Reconstruction policy. He later served as a diplomat in Dublin and president of Minnesota’s Macalester College. It was one of several Minnesota educational institutions that he had helped found. He also served as the state’s first superintendent of schools. He was devoted to the idea of education which taught Christian principles but unalterably opposed to co-education.

Vice President elected on 1860 Republican ticket but unexpectedly dropped on 1864 Union ticket in favor of Andrew Johnson, a Tennessee War Democrat. He had a cordial but not close relationship with the President. He exercised an important role in the selection of Lincoln’s first cabinet; he argued unsuccessfully against Seward’s inclusion in cabinet but was successful in naming Gideon Welles as New England’s cabinet representative. Hamlin played little role in President Lincoln’s first term, but did help win Mr. Lincoln’s agreement for the use of black soldiers. Hamlin was a strong supporter of Negro rights, before, during and after the Civil War. After the First Battle of Bull Run in July 1861, Hamlin became one of the first to pressure the President to pursue emancipation and recruitment of black soldiers as a strategy of war. He pushed for an immediate Proclamation of Emancipation in 1862.
White House etiquette did not even allow the Vice President regularly to attend cabinet meetings so unlike heads of departments, he seldom visited the White House—perhaps because he and Mary Todd Lincoln did not like each other. Aide William O. Stoddard noted: “It seems that a sort of etiquette has been established, in accordance with which it is not considered god taste for the second officer of the Republic to meddle much with public business, and which, at all events, keeps him away from the Executive Mansion.”1
Hamlin did not spend much more time in Washington during the war than necessary. He returned to Maine after his inauguration on March 4, 1861, proceeded to New York City after Fort Sumter fell, then returned to Maine, then back to New York and Washington. President Lincoln “was very busy, but treated me cordially and seemed pleased to see me. I think he is not sensible to just how he has treated me in certain matters, and I said nothing of it,” Hamlin wrote his wife. “He inquired particularly for you, and said his brief acquaintance with you was very pleasant, and he had formed a very high opinion of you. He must have known such kind words of my little wife were very gratifying to me – and they were.”2

[![Image 1: Edward Duffield Neill](https://www.mrlincolnswhitehouse.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/pf096062_med.jpg)](https://www.mrlincolnswhitehouse.org/residents-visitors/employees-and-staff/employees-staff-edward-duffield-neill-1823-1893/edward-duffield-neill/index.html)
Assistant secretary to President Lincoln (1864-65), Edward Duffield Neill was an ordained Presbyterian minister and dedicated historian. At the beginning of the Civil War, Rev. Neill served as chaplain to a Minnesota regiment and later as an army hospital chaplain in Philadelphia.
Neill took on William Stoddard’s land patent duties after William Stoddard became ill in mid-1864. Lincoln biographer Carl Sandburg wrote: “Chaplain Neill came to Lincoln’s office with a Vermont colonel seeking a brigadier general’s commission Lincoln had signed. The President had not returned from lunch. Neill was looking among papers on the President’s desk. The President came in eating an apple. ‘I told him for what I was looking,’ wrote Neill of this, ‘and as I talked he placed his hand on the bell-pull, when I said, ‘For whom are you going to ring?’ Placing his hand upon my coat, he spoke but two words, – ‘Andrew Johnson.’ Then I said, ‘I will come in again.’ As I was leaving the room the Vice President had been ushered in, and the President advanced and took him by the hand.’”1 Secretaries John G. Nicolay and John Hayclearly trusted Neill, who was older than both of them. Leaving to meet with Horace Greeley in mid-July 1864, Hay wrote Edward Neill: “I am going to New York tonight on business. Will be gone only a very few days”
> I leave matters in your hands till my return. There will probably be little to do. Refer as little to the President as possible. Keep visitors out of the house when you can. Inhospitable, but prudent.  
>   
>  I have a few franked envelopes. Let matters of ordinary reference go without formality of signature. If you have any doubt about any matter, please reserve it till my return.2
texts.1:
On the day President Lincoln was assassinated — April 14, 1865 — Neill saw President about a commission for the Freedman’s Bureau. He wrote later that “The President’s capacity for work was wonderful. While other men were taking recreation through the sultry months of summer he remained in his office attending to the wants of the nation. He was never an idler or a lounger. Each hour he was busy.”3
“Every month my impression of the greatness of President Lincoln increased. He was above a life of mere routine. In his bearing there was nothing artificial or mechanical,” wrote Neill. “He was independent of all cliques. Willing to be convinced, with a wonderful patience he listened to the opinions and criticisms of others.”4 Neill was also a chronicler of the President’s human side, writing on May 31, 1864: “Yesterday four or five thousand Sunday School children, with banner and bands of music[,] marched by the President’s House, while he stood at the window and received their hearty cheers with smiles…”5
Neill was a decade older than the older presidential assistants and had considerable experience in church and education affairs – while the primary assistants had a background in writing, journalism and politics. But like his colleagues, Neill was protective of the President.
texts.2:
> One morning he told his doorkeeper that he should not be interrupted as he was much engaged. Senator Howard of Michigan, came and said he must see him. The doorkeeper could not disobey orders, and brought him to me. As soon as he sat down, he showed that he was in ill humor, and said: ‘If it were his own son he would not act so.’ Never having seen the Senator, and supposing him to be some agent to procure substitutes, I replied that if he continued to speak disrespectfully of the President, in his own house, I must request him to leave the room. He then said that he was Senator Howard, and that he had come to request suspension of sentence of a soldier who in a few hours was to be executed.  
>   
>  Entering the President’s room, I found him very busy in writing, and apologetically said: ‘Would not have interrupted you, but Senator Howard wants suspension of sentence, in a certain case.’ ‘Wants suspension! Well, that is a queer request.’ Afterward he told me to write a telegram, giving the soldier’s name, ordering suspension of sentence, sign his name, and send it through the War Department. I told him I would write the order, but preferred that he should sign it.6
Neill remained at the White House as an aide to President Andrew Johnson. Unlike Stoddard, whom he replaced, Neill was a moderate on Reconstruction policy. He later served as a diplomat in Dublin and president of Minnesota’s Macalester College. It was one of several Minnesota educational institutions that he had helped found. He also served as the state’s first superintendent of schools. He was devoted to the idea of education which taught Christian principles but unalterably opposed to co-education.
